title: Data Management System Analysis for Distributed Computing Workloads
problem: Large-scale international collaborations (ATLAS) operate globally distributed workflow systems (PanDA) and data management systems (Rucio) with systemic inefficiencies: underutilized resources, redundant transfers, altered error distributions. Systems lack shared performance awareness and coordinated adaptive strategies.
motivation: ATLAS generates massive data volumes requiring coordination between workflow scheduling (PanDA) and data management (Rucio). Current systems optimize individually but fail to co-optimize at global scale. Inefficiencies accumulate across millions of jobs and petabytes of data movement.
method: The approach works by matching computing jobs (from PanDA) to their corresponding data files (in Rucio) using metadata—information about what data is stored where and what each job needs. It then identifies wasteful data transfer patterns across the global system that violate data-centric principles, such as moving the same file repeatedly when it could stay in place. Finally, it proposes coordination strategies to improve how the two systems work together and reduce unnecessary transfers.
key_novelty: This is the first systematic study of how a job scheduler (PanDA) and data management system (Rucio) interact globally, discovered by precisely matching individual computing jobs to their specific data files.
contributions: Metadata-matching algorithm linking jobs and datasets at file granularity
Complete view of data access and movement patterns across ATLAS distributed system
Identification of anomalous transfer patterns and root causes
Mitigation strategies and PanDA-Rucio coordination opportunities for tighter integration
limitations: Abstract-only; specific inefficiency magnitudes, mitigation effectiveness, and implementation status not provided.
